subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 5, SUBTOPIC A: FOOTBALL (SOCCER) (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic football skills
- explain the basic rules and common infringements of football
- identify player positions and their roles
- apply basic attacking and defending principles in football

BASIC SKILLS
1. Dribbling: moving the ball forward using a series of controlled touches with the feet, keeping the ball close so an opponent cannot easily win it; good dribbling uses both the inside and outside of the foot and includes changes of pace and direction to beat opponents.
2. Passing: sending the ball accurately to a teammate.
- Push pass (inside-of-foot pass): the most accurate short pass, using the inside of the foot to strike the ball firmly and directly.
- Instep/laces pass: used for longer, more powerful passes, striking the ball with the top of the foot (laces area).
- Outside-of-foot pass: used for quick, disguised passes in tight spaces.
3. Receiving/trapping: bringing an incoming ball under control using the foot (cushioning it on contact), thigh, chest, or occasionally the head, so the ball does not bounce away uncontrolled.
4. Shooting: striking the ball with power and/or accuracy toward the goal, often using the instep for power or the inside of the foot for placement/accuracy.
5. Heading: using the forehead (never the top of the head) to direct the ball, used for both attacking (heading toward goal) and defensive clearances.
6. Tackling: safely and fairly winning the ball from an opponent using the feet, timed correctly to avoid fouling.

PLAYER POSITIONS AND ROLES
- Goalkeeper: the only player allowed to handle the ball, but only within their own penalty area; responsible for preventing the opposing team from scoring.
- Defenders: players positioned mainly in their own half, responsible for stopping opposition attacks and regaining possession of the ball.
- Midfielders: players who link defence and attack, involved in both creating attacking opportunities and helping defend when possession is lost.
- Forwards/strikers: players positioned mainly in the opponent's half, primarily responsible for creating and finishing goal-scoring opportunities.

BASIC RULES
- A standard football match is played between two teams, each normally with a goalkeeper and outfield players (numbers may be adapted for younger/school-level games).
- A goal is scored when the whole of the ball crosses the goal line, between the goalposts and under the crossbar.
- Outfield players must not deliberately handle the ball with their hands or arms; only the goalkeeper may do so, and only inside their own penalty area.
- The game restarts with a kick-off at the start of each half and after a goal is scored.
- A throw-in is awarded to the opposing team when the ball fully crosses a touchline (sideline); it must be taken with both hands, from behind and over the head.
- A corner kick is awarded to the attacking team when the ball crosses the goal line (having last touched a defending player) without a goal being scored.
- A goal kick is awarded to the defending team when the ball crosses the goal line (having last touched an attacking player) without a goal being scored.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS (FOULS)
- Handling the ball deliberately (by an outfield player).
- Dangerous or reckless tackling, such as tackling with excessive force, from behind, or with the studs raised toward an opponent.
- Pushing, holding, tripping or charging an opponent unfairly.
- Offside: broadly, an attacking player being in an 'illegal' position (nearer to the opponent's goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender) at the moment the ball is played to them, though offside rules can be simplified or adapted for younger learners.
A foul results in a free kick (direct or indirect, depending on the nature of the foul) or, for a foul committed by a defender inside their own penalty area, a penalty kick to the attacking team.

BASIC ATTACKING PRINCIPLES
- Creating and moving into space rather than standing still or bunching together with teammates.
- Passing quickly and accurately to keep possession and unbalance the defending team.
- Supporting the player with the ball by offering passing options at different angles and distances.
- Taking shooting opportunities when in a good position, rather than delaying unnecessarily.

BASIC DEFENDING PRINCIPLES
- Marking opposing players closely to limit their space and passing options.
- Pressuring the player in possession of the ball to force mistakes or slow down their attack.
- Covering teammates, staying in a position to help if a teammate is beaten by an attacker.
- Communicating with teammates to organise defensive positioning as a team.

SUMMARY
- Core football skills include dribbling, passing, receiving, shooting, heading and tackling.
- Positions (goalkeeper, defenders, midfielders, forwards) each have distinct roles in attack and defence.
- Basic rules govern scoring, restarts (kick-off, throw-in, corner kick, goal kick) and handball.
- Common fouls include handling, dangerous tackling and offside, resulting in free kicks or penalties.
- Good attacking relies on space and quick passing; good defending relies on marking, pressure, covering and communication.

GLOSSARY
Offside: a rule preventing an attacking player from gaining an unfair advantage by being in an illegal advanced position when the ball is played to them.
Penalty kick: a direct free kick awarded to the attacking team for a foul committed by the defending team inside their own penalty area.
Marking: staying close to an opponent to limit their space, passing options or scoring chances.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 5

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 5, SUBTOPIC B: NETBALL (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic netball skills
- explain court areas and player positions in netball
- explain the basic rules and common infringements of netball
- apply basic attacking and defending principles in netball

BASIC SKILLS
1. Passing:
- Chest pass: the ball is held with both hands at chest height and pushed firmly and directly toward a teammate.
- Shoulder pass: a one-handed pass thrown from the shoulder, useful for longer or faster passes.
- Bounce pass: the ball is bounced once on the ground before reaching a teammate, useful for passing under an opponent's raised arms.
- Overhead pass: thrown from above the head, useful for passing over a defender who is close and low.
2. Catching: receiving the ball securely with both hands, fingers spread, absorbing the ball's speed by slightly 'giving' with the arms on catching.
3. Footwork: once a player catches the ball, whichever foot lands or is grounded first becomes the 'landing foot'; this foot cannot be lifted and re-grounded (dragged) while the player still holds the ball, though the player may pivot on it to change direction while keeping the other foot moving.
4. Shooting: performed only within the shooting circle by the Goal Shooter (GS) or Goal Attack (GA), using a controlled, arched shot aimed at the goal ring, with good balance and follow-through.
5. Dodging: quick changes of direction and speed used by a player without the ball to lose a defender and create space to receive a pass.

COURT AREAS AND PLAYER POSITIONS
A netball court is divided into thirds: two goal thirds (one at each end, each containing a shooting circle) and a centre third in the middle.
The seven playing positions, each restricted to specific areas of the court, are:
- Goal Shooter (GS): shoots for goals; allowed in the goal third (attacking) and shooting circle only.
- Goal Attack (GA): supports shooting and feeds the ball into the circle; allowed in the goal third (attacking), the shooting circle, and the centre third.
- Wing Attack (WA): feeds the ball to shooters; allowed in the centre third and the attacking goal third, but not inside the shooting circle.
- Centre (C): links defence and attack, allowed to move throughout the whole court except inside either shooting circle.
- Wing Defence (WD): marks the opposing Wing Attack; allowed in the centre third and the defending goal third, but not inside the shooting circle.
- Goal Defence (GD): marks the opposing Goal Attack; allowed in the goal third (defending), the shooting circle, and the centre third.
- Goal Keeper (GK): marks the opposing Goal Shooter and defends the goal; allowed in the goal third (defending) and shooting circle only.

BASIC RULES
- A goal is scored when the ball passes completely through the goal ring, and may only be shot from within the shooting circle by the GS or GA.
- Players may only move within the specific areas of the court permitted for their position.
- A player holding the ball must pass or shoot it within three seconds and may not run with it.
- Once a player lands with the ball, the landing foot cannot be lifted and re-grounded before releasing the ball (though pivoting on it is allowed).
- Contact, obstruction (standing too close, usually within 0.9m, to an opponent with the ball while attempting to intercept or defend) and pushing are not allowed.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS
- Footwork error: dragging or stepping with the landing foot while holding the ball.
- Held ball: holding the ball for longer than three seconds without passing or shooting.
- Obstruction: defending too closely to an opponent without the correct distance, or raising arms in a way that unfairly blocks a pass or shot.
- Contact: unfairly pushing, bumping or leaning on another player.
- Offside: moving into an area of the court not permitted for your position.

BASIC ATTACKING AND DEFENDING PRINCIPLES
Attacking: moving into open space to offer a passing option, using dodges to lose a marking defender, and passing quickly and accurately to keep the ball moving forward.
Defending: marking an opponent closely (while respecting the correct defending distance to avoid obstruction), intercepting passes where possible, and recovering position quickly if beaten.

SUMMARY
- Core netball skills include the chest, shoulder, bounce and overhead passes, catching, correct footwork, shooting and dodging.
- The court is divided into thirds, with seven playing positions each restricted to specific playing areas.
- Basic rules govern shooting (circle only), footwork, held ball (three-second) limits, and fair contact.
- Common infringements include footwork errors, held ball, obstruction, contact and moving offside.
- Good attacking uses space and dodging; good defending uses correct marking distance and quick recovery.

GLOSSARY
Landing foot: the first foot grounded by a player after catching the ball, which cannot then be dragged or re-grounded while holding the ball.
Obstruction: illegally standing too close to or blocking an opponent while defending or intercepting.
Shooting circle: the marked semicircular area at each end of a netball court from within which shots at goal must be taken.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 5

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 5, SUBTOPIC C: BASKETBALL (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic basketball skills
- explain the basic rules and common infringements of basketball
- describe basic player positions and their roles
- apply basic attacking and defending principles in basketball

BASIC SKILLS
1. Dribbling: bouncing the ball continuously with one hand while moving, keeping it low and close to the body for control, using fingertips (not the palm) to push the ball down.
2. Passing:
- Chest pass: pushed from the chest with both hands directly to a teammate.
- Bounce pass: bounced once on the floor before reaching a teammate, often used to pass under a defender's reach.
- Overhead pass: thrown from above the head, useful for passing over a nearby defender.
3. Catching/receiving: securing the ball with both hands, fingers spread, watching the ball into the hands.
4. Shooting:
- Set shot: a shot taken from a stationary position, using a smooth upward push with the shooting hand guided by the other hand, following through with the wrist snapping downward ('reaching into the cookie jar').
- Lay-up: a shot taken while moving toward the basket, taking off from one foot and releasing the ball softly off the backboard or directly into the ring at close range.
5. Pivoting: keeping one foot (the pivot foot) fixed on the floor while stepping in different directions with the other foot, used to protect the ball from defenders or find a passing/shooting angle without travelling.

BASIC PLAYER POSITIONS (TRADITIONAL)
- Point guard: typically the primary ball-handler, responsible for organising the team's attack and passing.
- Shooting guard/wing players: often responsible for scoring from the perimeter (outside shots) and supporting the point guard.
- Forwards: typically play closer to the basket, involved in both scoring and rebounding (recovering missed shots).
- Centre: usually the tallest player, playing close to the basket, important for rebounding and shot-blocking.
(At school level, positions are often more flexible, with all learners rotating through different roles.)

BASIC RULES
- A team scores two points for a basket made from open play, and one point for each successful free throw (awarded after certain fouls).
- A player in possession of the ball may not take more than the allowed number of steps without dribbling (travelling violation).
- Once a player stops dribbling, they may not start dribbling again without first passing or shooting (double dribble violation).
- The ball must be advanced up the court within a set time limit in formal rules (backcourt/time violations), though this is often simplified for school-level games.
- Personal fouls (illegal contact such as pushing, holding or charging into an opponent) result in a free throw or possession change for the opposing team, depending on the circumstances.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS
- Travelling: moving the pivot foot illegally, or taking too many steps, while holding the ball without dribbling.
- Double dribble: dribbling, stopping, and then dribbling again without passing or shooting in between.
- Personal foul: illegal physical contact with an opponent, such as pushing, holding, or blocking incorrectly.
- Held ball/jump ball: when two opposing players gain joint control of the ball at the same time, often restarted with a jump ball or alternating possession, depending on the level of play.

BASIC ATTACKING AND DEFENDING PRINCIPLES
Attacking: moving without the ball to create space and passing options, using pivoting to protect the ball from defenders, and taking good shooting opportunities close to or within a comfortable shooting range of the basket.
Defending: staying between the opponent and the basket, using quick footwork to stay in front of an attacking player, and contesting shots and passes without committing a foul.

SUMMARY
- Core basketball skills include dribbling, passing (chest, bounce, overhead), catching, shooting (set shot, lay-up) and pivoting.
- Basic positions include the point guard, shooting guard/wings, forwards and centre, each with different typical responsibilities.
- Basic rules cover scoring, travelling, double dribble and personal fouls.
- Good attacking uses movement and pivoting to create space and shooting chances; good defending uses positioning and footwork to stay between the attacker and the basket.

GLOSSARY
Travelling: an illegal movement of the feet while holding the ball without dribbling.
Double dribble: illegally dribbling again after having already stopped dribbling and held the ball.
Pivot foot: the foot a player keeps fixed on the ground while stepping with the other foot to protect the ball or change position.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 5

subject: Physical Education
topic: Invasion Games: Attacking and Defending Strategies
content:
TOPIC 5, SUBTOPIC D: ATTACKING AND DEFENDING STRATEGIES ACROSS INVASION GAMES (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- explain common attacking principles shared across invasion games
- explain common defending principles shared across invasion games
- apply simple tactical decision-making during small-sided games
- explain the values developed through participation in invasion games

WHY STUDY SHARED PRINCIPLES?
Although football, netball and basketball have different specific rules, they are all classified as invasion games because they share the same underlying tactical challenge: how to move an object into the opponent's territory to score, while preventing the opponent from doing the same. Because of this, many attacking and defending principles apply across all invasion games, even though the specific skills used (kicking, throwing, dribbling with hands) differ.

SHARED ATTACKING PRINCIPLES
1. Width: spreading out across the available playing space (rather than bunching together) makes it harder for defenders to cover every attacking option at once.
2. Depth: having attacking players positioned at different distances from the ball (some close, ready for a quick pass; some further forward, ready to receive a longer pass) gives more passing options.
3. Mobility: constantly moving into space, rather than standing still, makes it harder for defenders to predict and mark attacking players effectively.
4. Support: players without the ball moving into positions where they can be passed to easily, offering the ball-carrier multiple options.
5. Penetration: at the right moment, making a direct pass, dribble or run that moves the ball closer to the opponent's goal/scoring area, rather than only passing sideways or backward.
6. Quick, accurate decision-making: choosing the best available option quickly (pass, dribble, shoot) rather than hesitating, which gives defenders time to recover and organise.

SHARED DEFENDING PRINCIPLES
1. Marking: staying close enough to an opponent to prevent them from receiving a pass easily or shooting/scoring freely.
2. Delay: when unable to win the ball immediately, slowing down the attacking team's progress by staying goal-side (between the attacker and your own goal) rather than diving in recklessly.
3. Depth/cover: defenders positioning themselves to support each other, so if one defender is beaten, another can help stop the attack.
4. Balance: not all defenders committing to challenge the ball at once, keeping enough players back to cover different attacking threats.
5. Compactness: keeping the defending team relatively close together so there are no easy large gaps for attackers to exploit.
6. Communication: defenders talking to each other to organise who marks whom and to warn of oncoming attackers or passes.

APPLYING TACTICS IN SMALL-SIDED GAMES
Small-sided games (games played with fewer players than the full/formal version, on a smaller area) are commonly used in Physical Education lessons because they give each learner more touches of the ball, more decision-making opportunities, and clearer, more obvious examples of attacking and defending principles in action, compared to a full-sized formal game. When playing small-sided invasion games, learners should practise:
- recognising when to pass versus when to dribble/run with the ball
- recognising when to close down (pressure) an opponent versus when to hold a defensive position and delay
- communicating clearly and positively with teammates

VALUES AND LIFE SKILLS DEVELOPED THROUGH INVASION GAMES
- Teamwork: invasion games cannot be played successfully alone; learners must cooperate, support and communicate with teammates.
- Decision-making under pressure: invasion games require constant, quick decisions, developing a learner's ability to think and act quickly in changing situations.
- Fair play and respect: following rules, accepting officials' decisions, and respecting opponents, win or lose.
- Physical fitness: invasion games typically involve continuous movement, running, changes of direction and short bursts of speed, contributing to cardiovascular fitness, agility and coordination.
- Resilience: learning to recover from mistakes (a missed pass, a goal conceded) and continue contributing positively to the team.

SUMMARY
- Football, netball and basketball share the same core tactical challenge of invasion games, despite different specific rules and skills.
- Shared attacking principles include width, depth, mobility, support, penetration and quick decision-making.
- Shared defending principles include marking, delay, depth/cover, balance, compactness and communication.
- Small-sided games are a useful way to practise these shared principles with more involvement for each learner.
- Invasion games build teamwork, decision-making, fair play, fitness and resilience.

GLOSSARY
Penetration: an attacking pass, dribble or run that moves the ball meaningfully closer to the opponent's scoring area.
Delay: a defensive tactic of slowing an attacker's progress rather than immediately challenging for the ball.
Small-sided game: a game played with fewer players and/or on a smaller area than the full, formal version of the sport.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 5
